patient.name: Rajesh Patel
patient.complaint: Tiredness and breathlessness on the stairs for 3 months
background: Takes ibuprofen most days for knee osteoarthritis

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'most likely finding on blood tests': classify by MCV first, then use the clue (koilonychia, neuropathy, jaundice and splenomegaly, a drug or infection trigger, a mechanical valve) to name the type.

points: Rajesh, 67, is **exhausted** and puffed out on the stairs.
Occasional palpitations and light-headedness on standing.
No weight loss, no change in bowel habit.

steps.lead: Rajesh's tiredness came on slowly, so he has compensated. **MCV** will sort his anaemia into a group and point to the cause.
Fatigue, breathlessness, palpitations, dizziness and a **tachycardia** of 102: Rajesh has the general symptoms of any anaemia.

points: No jaundice, no splenomegaly, no lymph nodes.
Abdomen soft, no palpable mass; neurology normal.

steps.title: Rajesh's full blood count
steps.text: Microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with a reactive thrombocytosis. White cells and platelets are not low, so the marrow is working.

visual.title: MCV sorts the anaemia
visual.label: Rajesh 68
visual.caption: Below 80: microcytic. Think iron deficiency first.

steps.q: What is the most likely cause of Rajesh's anaemia?
steps.r: Microcytic with **koilonychia** and glossitis: **iron deficiency**. B12 is macrocytic; haemolysis causes jaundice and a high reticulocyte count.

steps.lead: Rajesh's MCV of 68 and koilonychia fit **iron deficiency**. In a 67 year old man on daily ibuprofen, the likely source is **GI blood loss**.

steps.title: Classify by MCV
head: Group
MCV
Main causes
Clue
rows: Chronic disease, acute bleed, CKD, haemolysis
Ferritin normal or high in chronic disease

steps.lead: Rajesh has no jaundice or splenomegaly and a low reticulocyte count, so he is **not haemolysing**. These are the other types the exam loves.

steps.title: Haemolytic and other anaemias: the clincher
head: Type
Clincher in the stem
Key test or film
rows: Mycoplasma, lymphoma, Raynaud's in the cold

steps.text: Iron deficiency in a **man or a post-menopausal woman** is GI blood loss until proven otherwise. Never just give iron without looking for the source.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (serum ferritin for iron deficiency, bone marrow biopsy for aplastic anaemia) and the next step for iron deficiency over 60 (FIT, then suspected cancer pathway).

steps.q: Which test best confirms Rajesh's iron deficiency?
steps.r: **Serum ferritin** below 30 µg/L diagnoses iron deficiency. Serum iron fluctuates and is low in chronic disease too.

steps.title: Rajesh's haematinics
steps.text: Low ferritin, low saturation, high TIBC: classic iron deficiency. Normal B12 and folate; coeliac negative.

steps.lead: Rajesh's ferritin of **6 µg/L** is well below the 30 cut-off: iron deficiency is confirmed.

visual.title: Serum ferritin
visual.label: Rajesh 6
visual.caption: Ferritin is also an acute-phase protein, so it can look normal or high in chronic disease.

steps.lead: Rajesh is **over 60** with iron deficiency, so he needs a **FIT** test, and referral on the suspected cancer pathway if it is positive.

points: Two-week-wait colonoscopy: ulcerated mass in the **caecum**.
Biopsy: adenocarcinoma; CT shows no spread.

visual.title: Where the silent bleed was
visual.caption: Right-sided (caecal) cancers ooze blood slowly, so they present as iron deficiency rather than a change in bowel habit.

steps.lead: Rajesh's white cells and platelets are normal. If he had **pancytopenia**, a **bone marrow aspirate and biopsy** would look for aplastic anaemia.

steps.text: Iron deficiency work-up: ferritin, then find the source. Over 60: **FIT**. Also check **coeliac serology**, and upper GI endoscopy where indicated.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (oral ferrous fumarate and treat the cause), what to do if oral iron is not tolerated or surgery is close (IV iron), transfusion when unstable, and specific treatments for warm AIHA and TTP.

steps.q: What should Rajesh start now, while his referral goes through?
steps.r: Stable iron deficiency: **daily oral ferrous fumarate**, plus treating the cause. He is not unstable, so no transfusion.

steps.lead: Rajesh's cancer is the cause to treat; **oral ferrous fumarate** replaces the iron meanwhile. His daily ibuprofen should also stop.

points: Two weeks later: nausea, black stools and **constipation** on the tablets.
Surgery for his caecal cancer is booked in **4 weeks**.

steps.lead: With **under 6 weeks** until his right hemicolectomy, oral iron is too slow. Rajesh gets **IV ferric carboxymaltose 1 g**, repeated a week later.

steps.title: Iron deficiency treatment
nodes: Side effects: alternate-day dosing, bulk-forming laxative
Not tolerated, not absorbing or surgery under 6 weeks: IV iron
Unstable or very low Hb: transfuse
steps.caption: Black stools on oral iron are expected; check the patient is otherwise well.

points: Ten days before surgery: dizzy, **fainted** at home.
Fresh blood mixed with stool today.

visual.title: Haemoglobin and the transfusion threshold
visual.label: Rajesh 61
visual.caption: Haemodynamically unstable with Hb 61: transfuse now.

steps.q: Rajesh is hypotensive with Hb 61 g/L. What does he need?
steps.r: Severe anaemia with **haemodynamic instability** needs **blood transfusion**. Iron takes weeks to raise the Hb.

steps.lead: Rajesh is transfused, then reassessed. In stable normocytic anaemia, give **1 unit** at a time and recheck, aiming for **Hb above 70**.

visual.title: Rajesh's haemoglobin
visual.caption: Transfusion rescues the crisis; iron and removing the cancer restore the Hb.

steps.lead: Rajesh's anaemia was blood loss. If he had **warm AIHA** he would get prednisolone; **TTP** needs urgent **plasma exchange**.

science.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely mechanism...?' for microcytosis (iron needed for haem), jaundice in haemolysis (unconjugated bilirubin), G6PD (NADPH and glutathione), schistocytes (mechanical shearing) and pancytopenia (stem cell failure).

steps.title: Why Rajesh's cells are small and pale

steps.lead: Rajesh's MCV of 68 and MCH of 21 are exactly this: **haem synthesis** has run out of iron.
Rajesh has a normal bilirubin and low reticulocytes. In haemolysis, broken-down haem raises **unconjugated bilirubin** and the marrow pours out reticulocytes.
G6PD makes **NADPH** to keep glutathione working. Without it, an oxidative trigger denatures haemoglobin into **Heinz bodies**.

steps.q: Which antibody and site of haemolysis is typical of warm AIHA?
o: IgG, mainly extravascular in the spleen
steps.r: **Warm: IgG**, splenic macrophages nibble the cells into **spherocytes**. **Cold: IgM** fixes complement in the cold, giving more intravascular haemolysis.

steps.lead: Rajesh does not have AIHA, but the exam tests the **IgG warm vs IgM cold** split and where the cells are destroyed.
A **mechanical valve**, TTP, HUS or DIC slices red cells as they pass, leaving **schistocytes** on the film. Rajesh's film shows none.
Rajesh's white cells and platelets are normal, so his stem cells are fine. Aplastic anaemia hits **all three lines**: pancytopenia.

steps.text: Reactive **thrombocytosis** is common in iron deficiency and active bleeding, as Rajesh's platelets of 452 show. It does not need treating.

mcq.q: What MCV defines a microcytic anaemia?
Which nail sign suggests iron deficiency?
mcq.r: Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails) is a sign of iron deficiency.

mcq.q: Which infection is associated with cold autoimmune haemolytic anaemia?
mcq.r: Cold AIHA (IgM) is linked to Mycoplasma pneumoniae and lymphoma.

mcq.q: What is the mode of inheritance of G6PD deficiency?
mcq.r: G6PD deficiency is X-linked recessive, so mostly affects males.

mcq.q: What serum ferritin level diagnoses iron deficiency?
mcq.r: Ferritin below 30 µg/L confirms iron deficiency.

mcq.q: Which blood film finding confirms a microangiopathic mechanism of haemolysis?
mcq.r: Schistocytes (fragmented red cells) confirm mechanical shearing.

mcq.q: A 66 year old has iron deficiency anaemia. What is the next investigation?
mcq.r: Over 60 with iron deficiency: FIT, then suspected cancer pathway if positive.

mcq.q: What is the first-line treatment for iron deficiency anaemia?
mcq.r: Daily oral ferrous fumarate, plus treat the cause.

mcq.q: What is the treatment for TTP?
mcq.r: TTP and other MAHA: plasma exchange.

mcq.q: Why does aplastic anaemia cause pancytopenia?
o: Destruction of pluripotent haematopoietic stem cells
mcq.r: All three cell lines fail because the stem cells are destroyed or suppressed.

technique.stem: A 71 year old man with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia has a 3 week history of tiredness and breathlessness. He is jaundiced and has splenomegaly. His pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg. Investigations show haemoglobin 78 g/L, raised reticulocytes, raised unconjugated bilirubin and raised LDH. A direct antiglobulin test is positive for IgG and the film shows spherocytes.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: is it haemolysis, and if so, which type?

clues: raised reticulocytes, raised unconjugated bilirubin and raised LDH
steps.x: Haemolysis screen positive, DAT positive with IgG, on a background of a lymphoproliferative malignancy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.**

elim: Cold AIHA is IgM, linked to Mycoplasma, worse in the cold.
G6PD is DAT negative, with Heinz bodies and bite cells after a trigger.
Hereditary spherocytosis is DAT negative and lifelong.
TTP shows schistocytes and low platelets, not spherocytes.

steps.x: **E. Warm AIHA.** DAT positive + IgG + spherocytes; CLL is the classic cause.

technique.stem: A 24 year old man has 3 weeks of tiredness, recurrent nosebleeds and two chest infections. He had a febrile illness with a rash 6 weeks ago. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. He has pallor and scattered bruises. There is no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly.
technique.q: Which investigation will confirm the diagnosis?

steps.x: Confirmatory investigation: first name the picture.

clues: recurrent nosebleeds and two chest infections
febrile illness with a rash 6 weeks ago
steps.x: Pancytopenia with low reticulocytes after a viral illness: marrow failure, probably **aplastic anaemia** (parvovirus B19).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bone marrow aspirate, with **bone marrow biopsy** as the confirmatory test (hypocellular marrow).

elim: Cultures look for infection, not the cause of pancytopenia.
CT looks for lymphoma or spread; there are no nodes or spleen.
DAT tests for autoimmune haemolysis, which would raise reticulocytes.
Ferritin tests iron stores and cannot explain low white cells and platelets.

steps.x: **B. Bone marrow biopsy.** Pancytopenia + low retics = look at the marrow.

technique.stem: A 58 year old woman has had black stools for 2 days and collapsed at home. She takes naproxen for arthritis. She is pale and clammy. Her pulse rate is 128 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. Investigations show haemoglobin 58 g/L (115–165).
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management of her anaemia?

steps.x: Initial management: is she stable?

clues: pulse rate is 128 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg
steps.x: Acute GI bleed, normocytic anaemia, **haemodynamically unstable**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Red cell transfusion** (alongside resuscitation and finding the bleed).

elim: B12 treats macrocytic deficiency anaemia.
IV iron works over weeks, too slowly for shock.
Oral iron is far too slow.
EPO is for CKD-related anaemia and is slow.

steps.x: **D. Red cell transfusion.** Unstable + severe anaemia = transfuse.

technique.stem: A 64 year old man had a mechanical aortic valve replacement 2 years ago. He has 2 months of tiredness and dark urine. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 136/62 mmHg. There is a metallic click and an ejection systolic murmur. The blood film shows fragmented red cells.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his anaemia?
o: Antibody-coated red cells removed by the spleen
Complement fixation by IgM in the cold
Oxidative damage from lack of NADPH

steps.x: Mechanism of the anaemia: start with the history.
Haemolysis with schistocytes and a negative DAT in a patient with a mechanical valve.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Red cells **sheared** by turbulent flow across the valve: mechanical haemolysis.

elim: Antibody-mediated splenic removal is warm AIHA; DAT is negative.
Stem cell failure gives low reticulocytes and pancytopenia.
IgM cold agglutinins give a positive DAT.
Lack of NADPH is G6PD deficiency, with Heinz bodies, not fragments.

steps.x: **D. Mechanical shearing.** Schistocytes = red cells cut up in the circulation.

practice.stem: A 44 year old woman has 4 months of tiredness and breathlessness on exertion. Her periods have been very heavy for a year. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. She has pale conjunctivae, angular stomatitis and spoon-shaped nails.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Microcytic anaemia with koilonychia in a woman with menorrhagia is iron deficiency. Thalassaemia trait is microcytic but does not cause koilonychia or heavy blood loss.

steps.x: Diagnosis: start with the MCV.
Menorrhagia (blood loss) plus koilonychia, with MCV 69.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Iron deficiency anaemia.**

elim: Chronic disease is usually normocytic with no blood loss source.
Pernicious anaemia is macrocytic.
Sideroblastic anaemia is rare, with high ferritin and a cause like lead or isoniazid.
Thalassaemia trait has no koilonychia and the Hb is usually only mildly low.

steps.x: **B. Iron deficiency anaemia.** Microcytic + koilonychia + blood loss.

practice.stem: A 59 year old woman with Hashimoto's thyroiditis has 6 months of tiredness and tingling in both feet. Her tongue is sore. She has reduced vibration sense at both ankles. Her pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Macrocytic anaemia with low B12, neuropathy, glossitis and intrinsic factor antibodies in a woman with another autoimmune disease is pernicious anaemia. Folate deficiency does not cause neurological signs.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a macrocytic anaemia.
Autoimmune background, neuropathy and glossitis with a high MCV.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pernicious anaemia** (autoimmune B12 deficiency).

elim: Alcohol causes macrocytosis but not low B12 or intrinsic factor antibodies.
Folate deficiency does not cause neuropathy.
Hypothyroidism gives a mild non-megaloblastic macrocytosis without low B12.
Myelodysplasia does not explain low B12 and positive antibodies.

steps.x: **E. Pernicious anaemia.** B12 deficiency = neurology; folate deficiency does not.

practice.stem: A 22 year old student is recovering from an atypical pneumonia treated with clarithromycin. Two weeks later he is tired and jaundiced, and his fingers turn white and painful when he goes outside in the cold. His pulse rate is 100 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Haemolysis with a positive DAT and Raynaud's after Mycoplasma pneumonia is cold AIHA (IgM). The raised MCV reflects reticulocytosis, not B12 deficiency.

steps.x: Diagnosis: haemolysis, then which type.

clues: white and painful when he goes outside in the cold
steps.x: Mycoplasma infection, Raynaud's in the cold, DAT positive.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cold autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.**

elim: G6PD is DAT negative.
Hereditary spherocytosis is DAT negative and lifelong.
The macrocytosis is from reticulocytes; B12 does not cause a positive DAT.
Warm AIHA is IgG, not linked to Mycoplasma or the cold.

steps.x: **A. Cold AIHA.** Mycoplasma + cold symptoms + DAT positive = IgM.

practice.stem: A 19 year old woman of Scottish descent has intermittent jaundice, worse when she has a cold. Her father had his spleen removed as a child. She has a palpable spleen. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. The blood film shows spherocytes and the direct antiglobulin test is negative.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Spherocytes with a negative DAT, splenomegaly and a family history of childhood splenectomy in a Northern European is hereditary spherocytosis (autosomal dominant). Warm AIHA also has spherocytes but a positive DAT.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a lifelong haemolytic picture.

clues: father had his spleen removed as a child
steps.x: Northern European, autosomal dominant family history, spherocytes, DAT negative.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hereditary spherocytosis.**

elim: G6PD is X-linked and shows Heinz bodies and bite cells.
Gilbert's causes jaundice but no anaemia or reticulocytosis.
Sickle cell gives painful crises and sickle cells on the film.
Warm AIHA is DAT positive.

steps.x: **C. Hereditary spherocytosis.** Spherocytes + DAT negative + family history.

practice.stem: A 26 year old man of Mediterranean origin is given nitrofurantoin for a urinary tract infection. Three days later he is tired, jaundiced and passing dark urine. His pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 122/68 mmHg. The film shows bite cells and Heinz bodies. The direct antiglobulin test is negative.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Acute haemolysis with Heinz bodies and bite cells after an oxidant drug (nitrofurantoin) in a man is G6PD deficiency (X-linked recessive). TTP would show schistocytes and low platelets.

steps.x: Diagnosis: what triggered this haemolysis?

clues: 26 year old man of Mediterranean origin
steps.x: Male, oxidant drug, Heinz bodies, DAT negative.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **G6PD deficiency.**

elim: Cold AIHA is DAT positive.
Spherocytosis shows spherocytes, not Heinz bodies.
PNH causes morning dark urine and thrombosis, not drug-triggered Heinz bodies.
TTP shows schistocytes, low platelets and neurology.

steps.x: **B. G6PD deficiency.** Oxidant trigger + Heinz bodies + bite cells.

practice.stem: A 62 year old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has 3 months of tiredness. She has active synovitis in both hands. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. There is no history of blood loss.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Normocytic anaemia with low serum iron, low transferrin saturation but high ferritin in active inflammation is anaemia of chronic disease. Iron deficiency needs a ferritin below 30.

steps.x: Diagnosis: MCV, then ferritin.
Chronic inflammation, normocytic, ferritin high but serum iron low.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Anaemia of chronic disease.**

elim: Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia.
Iron deficiency has a low ferritin and is usually microcytic.
Pernicious anaemia is macrocytic.
Sideroblastic anaemia is microcytic with high serum iron.

steps.x: **A. Anaemia of chronic disease.** Normocytic, low iron, normal or high ferritin.

practice.stem: A 35 year old woman has 2 months of tiredness. She eats a vegan diet and has heavy periods. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg. She has pale conjunctivae. A full blood count shows a microcytic anaemia.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Serum ferritin below 30 µg/L diagnoses iron deficiency anaemia. Transferrin saturation supports it but is less specific.

steps.x: Diagnostic test for the most likely cause.
Poor intake plus blood loss with microcytosis: iron deficiency.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Serum ferritin.**

elim: Marrow sampling is invasive and not needed for iron deficiency.
Electrophoresis is for thalassaemia if ferritin is normal.
B12 deficiency is macrocytic.
Transferrin saturation is supportive; ferritin is diagnostic.

steps.x: **C. Serum ferritin.** Below 30 µg/L = iron deficiency.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man has 3 months of tiredness. He has no change in bowel habit, no weight loss and no abdominal pain. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. Abdominal and rectal examinations are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: Repeat full blood count in 3 months
practice.e: Iron deficiency anaemia over 60 needs a FIT, with referral on the suspected cancer pathway if positive. CEA is not a diagnostic test.

steps.x: Next investigation once iron deficiency is proven.
Iron deficiency in a man over 60 with no bowel symptoms.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **FIT**, then the suspected cancer pathway if positive.

elim: Marrow biopsy is for unexplained cytopenias, not iron deficiency.
Waiting risks missing a cancer.
CEA is for monitoring, not diagnosis.
Ultrasound does not assess the bowel lumen.

steps.x: **B. Faecal immunochemical test.** Over 60 + iron deficiency = FIT.

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman has iron deficiency anaemia from menorrhagia, which is being treated by her gynaecologist. She has not had treatment for the anaemia. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. She is well and not breathless at rest.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management of her anaemia?
practice.e: Stable iron deficiency anaemia is treated with daily oral ferrous fumarate while the cause is addressed. IV iron is second-line.

steps.x: Initial management of stable iron deficiency.

clues: not had treatment for the anaemia
steps.x: Cause in hand, stable, no prior iron.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Daily oral ferrous fumarate.**

elim: B12 is for macrocytic deficiency.
IV iron is second-line.
Folate is for macrocytic deficiency.
She is stable; transfusion is for instability.

steps.x: **C. Oral ferrous fumarate daily.** Treat the cause, replace the iron.

practice.stem: A 52 year old woman with iron deficiency anaemia started daily oral ferrous fumarate 3 weeks ago. She has stopped taking it because of constipation and abdominal discomfort. She is otherwise well. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Stop iron and recheck in 6 months
Switch to alternate-day oral iron with a bulk-forming laxative
practice.e: If oral iron is not tolerated, first switch to every-other-day dosing and add a bulk-forming laxative. IV iron is second-line if this fails.

steps.x: Next step when first-line treatment causes side effects.

clues: stopped taking it because of constipation and abdominal discomfort
steps.x: Intolerance, not failure; she is stable.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Alternate-day dosing plus a bulk-forming laxative.**

elim: She is stable.
Stopping leaves her deficient.
B12 is the wrong deficiency.
IV iron comes after oral options fail, or before imminent surgery.

steps.x: **C. Alternate-day iron with a laxative.** Adjust before escalating.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man with iron deficiency anaemia from a sigmoid carcinoma is listed for surgery in 3 weeks. He is tired but stable. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management of his anaemia before surgery?
o: IV ferric carboxymaltose 1 g, repeated 1 week later
practice.e: With less than 6 weeks until surgery, IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose 1 g, repeated a week later) replaces stores fast enough. Oral iron is used if surgery is more than 6 weeks away.

steps.x: Pre-operative anaemia: how long until surgery?
Under 6 weeks to surgery, stable, iron deficient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV ferric carboxymaltose 1 g, repeated in 1 week.**

elim: Operating anaemic raises transfusion and complication risk.
Oral iron is too slow with under 6 weeks.
He is stable; transfusion is not first.
EPO is not first-line for iron deficiency.

steps.x: **A. IV ferric carboxymaltose.** Under 6 weeks to surgery = IV iron.

practice.stem: A 30 year old man develops jaundice and dark urine 2 days after eating a meal containing fava beans. His pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 120/70 mmHg. The blood film shows Heinz bodies and bite cells. The direct antiglobulin test is negative.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his haemolysis?
o: Complement fixation by IgM cold antibodies
Failure to generate NADPH to protect against oxidative damage
Splenic removal of IgG-coated red cells
practice.e: In G6PD deficiency, red cells cannot make NADPH to regenerate glutathione, so oxidative stress (fava beans) denatures haemoglobin into Heinz bodies; the spleen bites them out, leaving bite cells.

steps.x: Mechanism: name the condition, then the enzyme's job.
Oxidant trigger, Heinz bodies, not immune: **G6PD deficiency**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Without G6PD there is no **NADPH**, so glutathione cannot protect against oxidation.

elim: IgM complement fixation is cold AIHA and DAT positive.
Spectrin defects cause hereditary spherocytosis.
Shearing gives schistocytes, as in TTP.
IgG-coated cells are warm AIHA and DAT positive.

steps.x: **C. Failure to generate NADPH.** G6PD = oxidative haemolysis.

prompts.q: How is anaemia classified by MCV, with the main causes in each group?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the MCV is the first fork in every anaemia question.

points.p: Microcytic (below 80): iron deficiency, sideroblastic
points.why: Iron deficiency is by far the most common.

points.p: Normocytic (80–100): chronic disease, acute blood loss, CKD, haemolysis
points.why: Chronic disease has normal or high ferritin.

points.p: Macrocytic (above 100): B12 or folate deficiency, hypothyroidism
General symptoms: fatigue, pallor, breathlessness, palpitations, tachycardia
points.why: Severity depends on speed of onset.

prompts.q: What are the causes, signs and blood results of iron deficiency?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the source of loss and the nail sign.

points.p: Blood loss (GI bleed, menorrhagia), poor intake, malabsorption
points.why: In men and post-menopausal women, look for GI loss.

points.p: Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails)
Glossitis, conjunctival pallor, angular stomatitis
Low ferritin, low transferrin saturation, high TIBC
points.why: Chronic disease: low saturation but normal or high ferritin.

prompts.q: What are the features of haemolysis, and how do warm and cold AIHA differ?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: prove haemolysis, then DAT, then IgG or IgM.

points.p: Anaemia with jaundice and splenomegaly
Raised unconjugated bilirubin, LDH and reticulocytes
AIHA: DAT (Coombs) positive, spherocytes
points.why: Negative DAT points to a non-immune cause.

points.p: Warm: IgG, CLL/lymphoma, SLE, drugs (methyldopa, NSAIDs, cephalosporins)
Cold: IgM, Mycoplasma, lymphoma, Raynaud's in the cold
points.why: Raised MCV reflects reticulocytes, not B12 deficiency.

prompts.q: What are the features of pernicious anaemia, G6PD deficiency and hereditary spherocytosis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: each has one clincher in the stem.

points.p: Pernicious: autoimmune B12 deficiency (intrinsic factor/parietal cell antibodies)
points.why: Neuropathy and glossitis; links with Hashimoto's and type 1 diabetes.

points.p: G6PD: X-linked recessive, triggered by fava beans, nitrofurantoin, primaquine, infection
Hereditary spherocytosis: autosomal dominant, Northern European

prompts.q: What are microangiopathic, aplastic and sideroblastic anaemia, and their classic causes?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: schistocytes, pancytopenia, ring sideroblasts.

points.p: MAHA: schistocytes from shearing; TTP, HUS, DIC, mechanical valve
points.why: TTP pentad: fever, MAHA, low platelets, AKI, neurology.

points.p: HUS triad: haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, raised creatinine
points.why: Often after E. coli O157 diarrhoea in children.

points.p: Aplastic: stem cell damage, pancytopenia, after parvovirus B19 or SLE
Sideroblastic: microcytic with high ferritin, ring sideroblasts; lead or isoniazid

prompts.q: How is iron deficiency confirmed, and how do you investigate the cause over 60?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one number, one test, one pathway.

points.p: Serum ferritin below 30 µg/L
points.why: Ferritin is an acute-phase protein, so can be falsely normal.

points.p: Over 60: FIT test
FIT positive: suspected cancer pathway referral
Pancytopenia: bone marrow aspirate, biopsy confirms aplastic anaemia

prompts.q: How is iron deficiency anaemia treated, including before surgery?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: oral first, adjust for side effects, IV if time is short.

points.p: Treat the underlying cause
points.why: Iron alone does not fix a bleeding cancer.

points.p: Daily oral ferrous fumarate first-line
Not tolerated: alternate-day dosing plus bulk-forming laxative
Second-line: IV iron
Surgery under 6 weeks: IV ferric carboxymaltose 1 g, repeat 1 week later
points.why: Over 6 weeks: oral iron is enough.

prompts.q: When is transfusion needed, and how are warm AIHA, cold AIHA and TTP treated?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: unstable means blood; each haemolytic type has its own treatment.

points.p: Haemodynamic instability with severe anaemia: blood transfusion
1 unit at a time to keep Hb above 70
Warm AIHA: prednisolone ± rituximab, then immunosuppressants or splenectomy
Cold AIHA (severe): plasmapheresis
TTP/MAHA: plasma exchange

prompts.q: Why does iron deficiency cause small pale cells, and why does haemolysis cause jaundice?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: haem synthesis, then haem breakdown.

points.p: Iron is needed for haem synthesis
Insufficient haemoglobinisation: microcytic, hypochromic cells
Haemolysis releases haem, metabolised to unconjugated bilirubin
points.why: So jaundice without dark bile in the urine.

points.p: Marrow compensates with reticulocytosis; LDH rises from cell breakdown

prompts.q: Explain the mechanisms of G6PD haemolysis, warm vs cold AIHA, schistocytes and pancytopenia.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one mechanism per type.

points.p: G6PD makes NADPH to regenerate glutathione; oxidants cause Heinz bodies
points.why: Bite cells: spleen removes the Heinz bodies.

points.p: Warm AIHA: IgG, extravascular, splenic macrophages make spherocytes
Cold AIHA: IgM fixes complement, intravascular haemolysis
Schistocytes: shearing by fibrin/platelet microthrombi
Aplastic: pluripotent stem cell destruction, all three lines fail

glossary.Anaemia: A haemoglobin level below normal, reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.
glossary.MCV: Mean cell volume, the average red cell size; used to classify anaemia.
glossary.MCH: Mean cell haemoglobin, the average amount of haemoglobin per red cell; low in iron deficiency.
glossary.Microcytic: Red cells smaller than normal (MCV below 80 fL).
glossary.Normocytic: Red cells of normal size (MCV 80 to 100 fL).
glossary.Macrocytic: Red cells larger than normal (MCV above 100 fL).
glossary.Hypochromic: Red cells paler than normal because they contain less haemoglobin.
glossary.Ferritin: Protein that stores iron; its blood level reflects iron stores but rises with inflammation.
glossary.Transferrin saturation: Percentage of the iron-carrying protein transferrin that is loaded with iron.
glossary.TIBC: Total iron-binding capacity; rises in iron deficiency as the body makes more transferrin.
glossary.Koilonychia: Thin, spoon-shaped nails seen in iron deficiency.
glossary.Glossitis: Smooth, red, sore tongue from loss of papillae; seen in iron, B12 and folate deficiency.
glossary.Angular stomatitis: Cracks at the corners of the mouth, seen in iron deficiency.
glossary.Reticulocytes: Young red cells released from the marrow; raised when the marrow is compensating.
glossary.Reticulocytosis: Raised reticulocyte count, showing the marrow is making red cells faster.
glossary.LDH: Lactate dehydrogenase, an enzyme released from broken cells; raised in haemolysis.
glossary.Unconjugated bilirubin: Bilirubin not yet processed by the liver; rises when red cells break down.
glossary.Haemolysis: Premature destruction of red blood cells.
glossary.AIHA: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia: antibodies attack the patient's own red cells.
glossary.DAT: Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test, which detects antibody or complement on red cells.
glossary.Coombs test: Another name for the direct antiglobulin test.
glossary.Spherocytes: Small round red cells without central pallor; seen in warm AIHA and hereditary spherocytosis.
glossary.Schistocytes: Fragmented red cells from mechanical shearing in damaged vessels.
glossary.Heinz bodies: Clumps of denatured haemoglobin inside red cells, seen in G6PD deficiency.
glossary.Bite cells: Red cells with a 'bite' taken out where the spleen removed Heinz bodies.
glossary.Pappenheimer bodies: Iron-containing granules in red cells, seen in sideroblastic anaemia.
glossary.Ring sideroblasts: Red cell precursors with iron trapped in a ring around the nucleus; diagnostic of sideroblastic anaemia.
glossary.G6PD: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, an enzyme making NADPH to protect red cells from oxidation.
glossary.NADPH: Molecule that keeps glutathione in its active, protective form inside red cells.
glossary.Glutathione: Antioxidant that protects red cells from oxidative damage.
glossary.Pernicious anaemia: Autoimmune B12 deficiency from antibodies against intrinsic factor or gastric parietal cells.
glossary.Intrinsic factor: Stomach protein needed to absorb vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum.
glossary.Hereditary spherocytosis: Inherited red cell membrane defect making cells spherical and fragile; autosomal dominant.
glossary.MAHA: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia: red cells sheared in small damaged vessels.
glossary.TTP: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura: microthrombi causing MAHA, low platelets, fever, AKI and neurology.
glossary.HUS: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome: haemolytic anaemia, low platelets and kidney injury.
glossary.DIC: Disseminated intravascular coagulation: widespread clotting that uses up platelets and clotting factors.
glossary.Aplastic anaemia: Failure of bone marrow stem cells, causing low red cells, white cells and platelets.
glossary.Pancytopenia: Low red cells, white cells and platelets together.
glossary.Parvovirus B19: Virus causing 'slapped cheek' rash that can temporarily stop red cell production.
glossary.Sideroblastic anaemia: Anaemia where iron is present but cannot be used to make haem.
glossary.Thrombocytosis: Raised platelet count; often reactive in iron deficiency or bleeding.
glossary.FIT: Faecal immunochemical test, detecting hidden blood in stool to screen for bowel cancer.
glossary.Ferrous fumarate: Oral iron tablet, first-line treatment for iron deficiency anaemia.
glossary.Ferric carboxymaltose: Intravenous iron preparation that replaces iron stores quickly.
glossary.Plasma exchange: Removing the patient's plasma and replacing it with donor plasma; treatment for TTP.
glossary.Plasmapheresis: Removing plasma from the blood to clear harmful antibodies.
glossary.Rituximab: Antibody drug that depletes B cells; used in warm AIHA.
glossary.Raynaud's phenomenon: Fingers turning white, blue then red in the cold from blood vessel spasm.
glossary.Mycoplasma pneumoniae: Bacterium causing atypical pneumonia; associated with cold AIHA.
glossary.CLL: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, a common cause of warm AIHA.
glossary.Anaemia of chronic disease: Normocytic anaemia in long-term inflammation with low serum iron but normal or high ferritin.
